config.title: Design DataTable API

intro.title: Design DataTable API
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a DataTable component API by designing its props to accept data and configuration options. You will learn how to structure a component's interface to make it reusable and flexible for different datasets. The core concept involves using React props to pass data and functions, such as an array of objects for rows and an array for column definitions. You'll work with JavaScript objects, arrays, and JSX to create a table that dynamically renders based on the provided props.
intro.usecase: DataTable APIs are essential for building enterprise dashboards, admin panels, and analytics tools where users need to sort, filter, and paginate large datasets. You'll find them in products like Salesforce's customer management interface, Shopify's order administration panels, and financial reporting dashboards where users interact with tabular data. As a developer, you'll implement these APIs to handle complex data operations while maintaining responsive UI performance. This pattern is crucial for any application displaying searchable, sortable tables with server-side data processing requirements.

objectives: Construct a DataTable component with a configurable API interface
Initialize and manage state for table data and configuration options
Implement sorting functionality through column header click handlers
Configure pagination controls to manipulate displayed data subsets
Apply filtering logic to dynamically update table content
Bind event handlers to user interactions for table operations
Render conditional UI elements based on data and configuration states

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary React imports to start building your DataTable component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports aren't quite right. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create DataTable component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named DataTable that returns null initially.
steps.hint: Define a function called DataTable that returns null. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your DataTable component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A DataTable component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: A functional component named DataTable exists and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the DataTable component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have a component named DataTable that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined a component named DataTable that returns null.

steps.title: Define component props
steps.instruction: Add a props parameter to your DataTable component with 'data' and 'columns' properties.
steps.hint: In the component function signature, add parentheses with (props) or destructure directly with ({ data, columns }).
steps.expectedOutcome: The DataTable component now accepts props with data and columns properties.
successCriteria: DataTable component has a props parameter that includes data and columns.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added props, but make sure to include both 'data' and 'columns' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should accept props with data and columns properties. Check the function signature.

steps.title: Initialize table state
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called sortConfig initialized to null.
steps.hint: Call useState(null) and destructure the returned array into sortConfig and setSortConfig.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a sortConfig state variable ready to track sorting configuration.
successCriteria: sortConfig state is declared using useState with null as initial value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState with null as the initial value and naming the variable sortConfig.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the DataTable component, use useState to create a state variable called sortConfig initialized to null.

steps.title: Create sorting handler
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component, define a function named handleSort that takes a columnKey parameter and updates the sortConfig state.
steps.hint: The handleSort function should toggle between ascending and descending order when the same column is clicked again.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleSort function that updates the sortConfig state based on the column key clicked.
successCriteria: The handleSort function is defined inside the DataTable component and updates the sortConfig state with the correct key and direction.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleSort function properly updates the sortConfig state based on the column key.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSort function isn't defined correctly. It should update the sortConfig state when called with a column key.

steps.title: Add table container
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component, return a <table> element with the className 'data-table'.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement (return null) with a table element that has the specified class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a table element with the correct class name, establishing the main table structure.
successCriteria: The DataTable component returns a <table> element with className 'data-table'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a <table> element with exactly className='data-table'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this step: return a <table> element with className 'data-table' from your DataTable component.

steps.title: Add table header
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component's return statement, add a <thead> element containing a <tr> with three <th> elements for 'ID', 'Name', and 'Age' columns.
steps.hint: The <thead> should be placed inside the <table> element you created earlier. Each <th> represents a column header.
steps.expectedOutcome: The table will have a header row with three column headers: ID, Name, and Age.
successCriteria: The component returns a <table> containing a <thead> with a <tr> that has three <th> elements with the text 'ID', 'Name', and 'Age'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly three <th> elements with the correct text content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The table header structure is incomplete or incorrect. Check that you have <thead> containing <tr> with three <th> elements.

steps.title: Wire sort handler to headers
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component, add an onClick handler to each th element that calls handleSort with the appropriate column key.
steps.hint: Use onClick={() => handleSort('columnKey')} on each th element. You'll need to decide what column key to pass for each header.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each table header cell (th) will have an onClick handler that triggers the sorting functionality when clicked.
successCriteria: All th elements have onClick handlers that call handleSort with appropriate column keys.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some onClick handlers, but not all th elements have them yet. Make sure each header cell has its own onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The onClick handlers are missing or incorrectly implemented. Each th element needs an onClick that calls handleSort with a column key.

steps.title: Add table body
steps.instruction: Inside your DataTable component, add a tbody element after the thead that maps through the data state to create table rows (tr) with cells (td) for each item.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the data array to generate a tr for each row, and inside each row create td elements for each property (name, age, email).
steps.expectedOutcome: The table will have a tbody section that displays rows of data, with each row containing cells for name, age, and email.
successCriteria: A tbody element is added that maps through the data state to generate tr elements, each containing three td elements for name, age, and email.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a tbody, but make sure it maps through the data array and includes all three cells (name, age, email) per row.
steps.feedbackWrong: The table body is missing or incomplete. Add a tbody that maps through data to create rows with cells for each property.

steps.title: Populate table cells
steps.instruction: Inside the table body, map through each row's data to create table cells (td elements) that display the corresponding values for each column.
steps.hint: Use the map function on the rows array to create tr elements, then inside each row map through columns to create td elements with the row data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The table body will be populated with rows and cells showing the actual data values for each column.
successCriteria: The table body contains tr elements for each row, with td elements inside that display row[column.key] values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're mapping through both rows and columns to create all the necessary td elements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The table body isn't properly populated. Make sure you're creating tr elements for each row and td elements for each column with the correct data values.
